{"id": "37:140/q11", "question": "How was Jonah selected and put overboard?", "turns_on": "Accounts vary in why the lot was held, how many times it was drawn, and whether the crew cast him, he jumped into the sea, or he entered the fish's mouth.", "positions": [{"id": "37:140/q11/p1", "position": "The crew cast lots, often three times, selecting Jonah, who confessed his flight and went into the sea.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Jonah first identified himself; the crew refused to cast God's messenger overboard, then drew names in water three times and found his name each time. Ibn ʿAbbās and Wahb in al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī say he admitted being the runaway and jumped; al-Wāḥidī's Wahb says he threw himself in after the lot. Tawus reports three lots and his jump. Ibn Kathīr says the crew resisted despite three losses and Jonah stripped to jump. Al-Wāḥidī's Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says Jonah confessed a grave sin and proposed a lot before they cast him overboard. Al-Māwardī says the crew suspected a sinner and chose him by lot. Al-Ālūsī reports three selections followed by casting him overboard. Islahi says the crew wanted the apparent sinner removed; Asad says Jonah agreed to the lot. In the biblical accounts reported by al-Biqāʿī, Elmalılı, Kur'an Yolu, and the Study Quran, the storm prompted lots, Jonah confessed or requested casting overboard, and the sea calmed afterward in the Study Quran's account. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the biblical sailors' cargo throwing and lot."}, {"id": "37:140/q11/p2", "position": "Lots selected Jonah as an offering to a great fish so the vessel could escape.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the crew cast him into the sea, the fish swallowed him, and the ship escaped. Ḥumayd ibn Hilāl says Jonah asked to be tipped feet first; a pale-mouthed whale swallowed him and a larger whale followed."}, {"id": "37:140/q11/p3", "position": "He jumped himself into the fish's mouth when it rose by God's command.", "reasons": "The Study Quran attributes this to some Quranic commentators reported by IK and says the sailors hesitated to throw him."}]}
{"id": "37:140/q12", "question": "What happened to Jonah in and after the fish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "37:140/q12/p1", "position": "God preserved Jonah in the fish, which ultimately returned him unharmed to shore.", "reasons": "Muqātil says God had not instructed the whale before Jonah's fall; at two spans above the water God made its belly a place of worship, forbade harm to hair or skin, and forbade food or drink. Water and wind challenged Jonah's flight, affirmed their worship and fear of God, and he recalled his deeds until inspired to call. Al-Qurṭubī cites al-Zamakhsharī's report of a whale swimming beside the ship with Jonah breathing and praising from its raised head, then carrying him ashore unharmed. Al-Biqāʿī's translated Book of Jonah says he prayed after three days and nights in the great fish; Kur'an Yolu's biblical summary says he prayed, was returned ashore and recommissioned. Kur'an Yolu cites 21:87–88 for prayer and rescue; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the Quranic account proceeds through fish, rescue, renewed mission and belief."}]}
{"id": "37:140/q13", "question": "How long did Jonah remain in the fish?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted durations are reported without an argument selecting one.", "positions": [{"id": "37:140/q13/p1", "position": "Three days, or three days and nights.", "reasons": "The Study Quran lists three days among competing accounts; al-Biqāʿī's translated Book of Jonah says his prayer came after three days and nights."}, {"id": "37:140/q13/p2", "position": "Seven days.", "reasons": "Listed as one of the different accounts by the Study Quran."}, {"id": "37:140/q13/p3", "position": "Forty days.", "reasons": "Listed as one of the different accounts by the Study Quran."}, {"id": "37:140/q13/p4", "position": "From morning until evening of the same day.", "reasons": "The Study Quran gives a report of swallowing in the morning and expulsion that evening."}]}
{"id": "37:140/q14", "question": "What does Jonah's flight imply about prophetic fault and servitude?", "turns_on": "Whether the Quranic terms assign an actual fault to a prophet or describe only the apparent implication of his act.", "positions": [{"id": "37:140/q14/p1", "position": "He left a divine duty without leave and was blameworthy for a lapse of impatience or desire.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says he opposed God's command. Al-Jishumī says he was obliged to continue calling until God ordered departure. Al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm says genuine servitude abandons desire and gives itself for God's affairs; Jonah chose desire over self-sacrifice, and despite aiming for the right course missed God's intended one. Islahi says a prophet cannot leave his post even with a pious motive and describes being cast into the sea as punishment. Kur'an Yolu calls the regretted act a momentary angry lapse for which he suffered, cites 68:48–50 on impatience, and reports a long frustrated preaching period."}, {"id": "37:140/q14/p2", "position": "The descriptions of flight and anger convey how his conduct appeared, while the prophet committed no sin.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī holds that, unlike biblical scriptures allowing even major prophetic sins, the Quran exempts prophets from major and minor sin; descriptions of absconding, anger and supposing God could not constrain him in 21:87 therefore express the apparent implication of his action. He rejects the biblical account's account of fleeing the commission and resenting a saved people despite knowing their repentance."}]}
{"id": "37:140/q15", "question": "What lesson does Jonah's departure teach about a prophet's mission?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "37:140/q15/p1", "position": "A prophet must persist until God releases him, since only God knows when a people have received conclusive warning.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says Jonah should have continued calling until commanded to leave. Islahi says prophets must endure their ordained trials, an attempted escape may bring a greater trial, the nation needs respite until truth is fully communicated, and only God knows when that is; passion for truth can make prophets exceed bounds, which God checks because they serve as a barometer of truth. Kur'an Yolu says extraordinary events trained prophets for difficult monotheist struggles."}]}
{"id": "37:140/q16", "question": "How does this episode fit the sūra's telling of the prophets?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "37:140/q16/p1", "position": "It illustrates the burdens of messengership and God's care and support for His chosen messengers.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says it consoles the Prophet against Quraysh's arrogance and shows that God does not abandon messengers even when they try to flee their charge. Islahi says the prophet stories share refrains of peace, mercy, support for the mission and reward for good deeds; prophets through Aaron are chronological, thereafter ordered by their attributes. Kur'an Yolu says these verses privilege the story's lesson over bare history. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says al-Ṣāffāt recounts selected stages: mission, departure, ship, fish, rescue, renewed mission and the people's belief."}]}
{"id": "37:140/q17", "question": "How does this compressed account connect to other scriptural tellings?", "turns_on": "Whether and how the fuller biblical narrative may be used alongside the Quranic account, especially on Jonah's knowledge and prophetic commission.", "positions": [{"id": "37:140/q17/p1", "position": "Other Quranic passages supply or recall parts of Jonah's story omitted here.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī connects his departure with going away angry at 21:87 and notes that discussion of idh follows two earlier stories. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says events between departure and the ship are omitted for concision; Abū Ḥayyān says al-Anbiyāʾ fills gaps before the ship and before prayer in the darkness. Ibn al-Jawzī refers back to discussions at the end of Yūnus and al-Anbiyāʾ 86; Ibn Kathīr recalls al-Anbiyāʾ. Asad points to 21:83. Islahi says Jonah's account also occurs in Yūnus and Anbiyāʾ and alleges Torah narrators distorted it. Kur'an Yolu notes his inclusion among revelatory prophets in 4:163 and in the seventeen listed at 6:86, the people's repentance in 10:98, his prayer and rescue in 21:87–88, and rebuke and favor in 68:48–50. The Prophet's report in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections, cited by Ibn Kathīr, forbids claiming superiority over Yunus ibn Mattā; the lineage is given through his mother, with a variant making Mattā his father."}, {"id": "37:140/q17/p2", "position": "The biblical account offers a fuller parallel with both agreements and disputed features.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī's translated Book of Jonah gives commission to Nineveh, ship flight, storm, lot, sea, great fish, and prayer after three days and nights. Elmalılı and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī report the Tarshish voyage via Jaffa through al-Ālūsī; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds discarded cargo, a sleeping Jonah and the captain waking him. Kur'an Yolu says the Bible broadly matches the Qur'an, ending with prayer, shore, recommission and Nineveh's repentance. The Study Quran adds the tempest, Jonah's identification by lot, and a calmed sea after he was thrown. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the biblical attribution of fleeing an ongoing commission and resenting spared believers despite knowledge of their repentance; Islahi also says Torah narrators distorted the account."}]}

{"id": "37:141/q03", "question": "Why did the people aboard draw lots?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over whether the ship stalled, a storm exposed a hidden offender, or its occupants sought to reduce the load by sacrificing one person.", "positions": [{"id": "37:141/q03/p1", "position": "A stalled ship led them to seek the guilty, fugitive, or ill-omened passenger.", "reasons": "Yahya, Qatada, Said ibn Jubayr, Wahb, Ibn Atiyya, Tawus, and others say the vessel would not move; Ibn Atiyya says other ships sailed on. Al-Bursevi says there was no wind or apparent cause, while merchants cited prior experience. The suspected fault is variously called wrongdoing, a grave sin, an escaped servant, an ill-omened man, or a criminal. Ibn Jawzi's Ibn Masud report says Jonah's people had repented after a three-day warning. The biblical Book of Jonah says the lot identified the cause of a calamity."}, {"id": "37:141/q03/p2", "position": "A storm or threatened sinking prompted a draw to identify its cause.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari's account reports a violent storm and suspected passenger; the Biblical narratives related by al-Biqai, Elmali, Tabatabai, Asad, and Study Quran likewise make the storm the occasion, with Jonah's flight identified by lot. Tabatabai says sailors first threw cargo overboard and Jonah was woken from sleep."}, {"id": "37:141/q03/p3", "position": "Facing sinking, they drew lots to sacrifice one passenger and save the rest or lighten the vessel.", "reasons": "A report in al-Tabrisi explicitly gives the belief that throwing one overboard saves the rest. Ibn Kathir says waves threatened the ship and the passenger was to lighten it; al-Bursevi reports the merchants' calculation that one loss was better than all. Tabatabai says the lot selected someone for a great fish, allowing the ship to escape. Ibn Ashur says ancient seafarers used lots when passengers or cargo overloaded a ship."}]}
{"id": "37:141/q04", "question": "What did Jonah and the sailors do before the draw?", "turns_on": "Reports differ on Jonah's confession, prayer during the storm, and attempted jump before the lot.", "positions": [{"id": "37:141/q04/p1", "position": "Jonah identified himself as the fugitive or sinner and proposed that he be thrown overboard.", "reasons": "Muqatil says the sailors refused because Jonah was God's messenger. {"id": "37:141/q06", "question": "What does al-mudḥaḍīn mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the participle describes the loser selected by lot, anyone assigned a lot, or the related idiom of a defeated argument.", "positions": [{"id": "37:141/q06/p1", "position": "Those defeated in the drawing of lots: Jonah's lot selected him as the loser.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Tabari, al-Farra, al-Jishumi, al-Tabrisi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, al-Biqai, al-Bursevi, and al-Alusi connect defeat with slipping or falling from victory; the root also describes an invalidated argument. Al-Tabari notes that the idiom of God making a proof slip is uncommon. Abu Qays's poem supports 'defeated'; Dhu al-Isba's verse, an unnamed camel poem, and al-Qurtubi's anonymous poetic line illustrate slippery ground or the vanquished. Ibn Faris and al-Burhan say the root usually denotes falsehood, while this verse uses defeat. Some glosses stress selection by lot or expulsion from the ship; Elmali says consent remains possible. Al-Suddī's and Ibn Abbas's reports use selection; Ibn Uyayna calls it losing the gamble."}, {"id": "37:141/q06/p2", "position": "Those who participated in or were assigned a lot.", "reasons": "Mujahid is reported as calling them those assigned a lot and elsewhere those who drew lots; the emphasis is on participation or assignment rather than defeat."}, {"id": "37:141/q06/p3", "position": "A refuted or invalidated argument.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi derives this gloss from the usage of making an argument fail. {"id": "37:141/q07", "question": "What is the root image behind al-mudḥaḍīn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "37:141/q07/p1", "position": "Slipping or falling on wet, muddy, or otherwise slippery ground.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda cites Dhu al-Isba's poem about daḥḍ ground and the idiom adḥaḍa ḥujjatahu. {"id": "37:141/q15", "question": "When and for what may drawing lots settle a matter?", "turns_on": "The issue is the permitted scope of a lot: fair allocation of an uncertain entitlement, every ambiguity, or selecting a person for lethal sacrifice.", "positions": [{"id": "37:141/q15/p1", "position": "Drawing lots is lawful for uncertain allocations.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Arabi says lots existed in earlier law and Islamic law, citing 3:44; the Prophet drew among wives for travel, among six slaves for deathbed manumission, and directed inheritance disputants to draw. Al-Alusi and jurists he reports cite Jonah's story; al-Sadiq says entrusting the draw to God yields the true, fairest lot."}, {"id": "37:141/q15/p2", "position": "Lots should govern every ambiguous case, including which wife is divorced.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Arabi argues lots most clearly resolve uncertainty and settle judgment; divorce among wives follows by analogy with selecting enslaved women for manumission."}, {"id": "37:141/q15/p3", "position": "Lots may not choose a person to be thrown into the sea, even to lighten a ship.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi treats Jonah's case as a unique preliminary to manifest proof and strengthen faith, not precedent for killing or throwing a sinner into fire or water. {"id": "37:142/q02", "question": "How did Jonah come to be swallowed?", "turns_on": "The accounts differ on whether Jonah leapt, was cast in, or was caught before reaching the water.", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q02/p1", "position": "He jumped into the sea and the waiting fish swallowed him.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says the fish opened its mouth at every side of the ship; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says it waited for God's command. {"id": "37:142/q05", "question": "Where did the fish come from or carry Jonah?", "turns_on": "The transmitted routes differ; Ibn ʿĀshūr disputes a Tigris location for Jonah's drowning.", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q05/p1", "position": "Najm carried Jonah through the Sea of Rome, the Nile, Persia, and the Tigris.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports this from Qatāda."}, {"id": "37:142/q05/p2", "position": "It took him past Eilat and returned by the Tigris to Nineveh.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this without a named authority."}, {"id": "37:142/q05/p3", "position": "It toured all seas and cast him on the Tigris bank.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's seven-day journey."}, {"id": "37:142/q05/p4", "position": "It came from Yemen and carried him to the lowest earth.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites Kashf al-Asrār; Jonah heard stones glorifying God there."}, {"id": "37:142/q05/p5", "position": "It came from the far end of the seas to the passing ship.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites Kāshifī: God inspired it to open its mouth."}, {"id": "37:142/q05/p6", "position": "Jonah's drowning took place in the Mediterranean Sea of Rome.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr locates the event there and rejects some exegetes' claim of the Tigris."}, {"id": "37:142/q05/p7", "position": "Jonah's drowning took place in the Tigris.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this as a view of some exegetes and rejects it; other reports have the fish carry him to the Tigris."}]}
{"id": "37:142/q06", "question": "What was the fish ordered to do with Jonah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q06/p1", "position": "Swallow and shelter him without eating or injuring him; its belly was a prison, refuge, or place of worship.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says God prohibited eating and drinking him. {"id": "37:142/q07", "question": "How long was Jonah in the fish?", "turns_on": "Reported spans range from part of a day to forty days; Ibn Kathīr does not decide.", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q07/p1", "position": "Part of a day, morning or midday to evening, with no night.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbī is reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Māwardī, al-Baghawī, al-Durr, and Ibn Kathīr through Mujālid; Ibn Kathīr says God knows. Al-Ṭabarī's Saʿīd ibn Jubayr report has ejection at sunset after prayer."}, {"id": "37:142/q07/p2", "position": "One hour of daylight.", "reasons": "One group in Ibn ʿAṭiyya."}, {"id": "37:142/q07/p3", "position": "Seven hours.", "reasons": "Another group in Ibn ʿAṭiyya."}, {"id": "37:142/q07/p4", "position": "Three days, or three days and nights.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān give three days; the biblical report gives days and nights, relayed by al-Biqāʿī, Elmalılı, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī."}, {"id": "37:142/q07/p5", "position": "Seven days or a week.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Jaʿfar, ʿAṭāʾ, and Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq are reported; Saʿīd adds a tour of all seas and ejection at the Tigris."}, {"id": "37:142/q07/p6", "position": "Fourteen days.", "reasons": "A group in Ibn ʿAṭiyya."}, {"id": "37:142/q07/p7", "position": "Twenty days.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī reports al-Ḍaḥḥāk."}, {"id": "37:142/q07/p8", "position": "Forty days or nights.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says nights; Abū Mālik, al-Suddī, al-Kalbī, Muqātil ibn Sulaymān, and Ibn Jurayj are reported for forty days."}, {"id": "37:142/q07/p9", "position": "Days and nights, without an exact count.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says he was preserved alive and well; Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt's verse speaks of nights in the fish."}]}
{"id": "37:142/q08", "question": "What did Jonah do in the fish, and how was he rescued?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q08/p1", "position": "He prayed, God answered, and the fish cast him out.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā cites 21:87–88 and identifies the three darknesses as night, sea, and belly. {"id": "37:142/q09", "question": "What does “mulīm” mean?", "turns_on": "The senses differ on culpable action, external blame, self-blame, defect, and surrender.", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q09/p1", "position": "He had done wrong or something deserving blame: a sinner or blameworthy person.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda, Ibn Zayd, Ibn ʿAbbās and others say sinner or wrongdoer. Al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās and others define alāma as doing what merits blame. Labīd's ghayr mulīm and Umayya's poetic line witness usage. Al-Ṭabarī distinguishes mulīm, whose act merits blame even without spoken reproach, from malūm, verbally blamed whether deserved or not; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites him and al-Qurṭubī."}, {"id": "37:142/q09/p2", "position": "He surrendered himself to his Lord.", "reasons": "Muqātil gives this and returns to it after citing al-Farrāʾ; al-Wāḥidī reports the same gloss."}, {"id": "37:142/q09/p3", "position": "He blamed himself for what he did.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports Qatāda; al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī give this sense. Bursevī treats the hamza as causative; al-Ālūsī says its object is omitted. Elmalılı adds regret."}, {"id": "37:142/q09/p4", "position": "He was blamed, whether or not he deserved it.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and Bursevī include this sense; al-Samīn quotes an anonymous poem using mulīm for one blamed without sin."}, {"id": "37:142/q09/p5", "position": "He was blemished or made defective by his act.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī offers blemished and says lāma can describe making oneself defective through an act; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites him."}]}
{"id": "37:142/q10", "question": "What is the form of “mulīm,” and why use it?", "turns_on": "How the active form and hamza convey culpability or self-blame.", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q10/p1", "position": "It is the active form of alāma, showing Jonah as agent of the blameworthy cause.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an active participle. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts mulīm with malūm and surveys cognates in 51:54, 17:29, 17:39, 70:30, 23:6, 12:32, 14:22, 68:30, 5:54, and 75:2."}, {"id": "37:142/q10/p2", "position": "Alāma can mark entering blame, becoming blameworthy, or causatively blaming oneself.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī assigns these functions to the three glosses; Bursevī reserves the causative hamza for self-blame."}]}
{"id": "37:142/q11", "question": "Is there a variant reading of “mulīm”?", "turns_on": "The first vowel and whether the form is active or an exceptional passive of a wāw-root.", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q11/p1", "position": "The usual mulīm has ḍamma and is an active form from alāma.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly calls it active; al-Naḥḥās and al-Samīn derive it from alāma."}, {"id": "37:142/q11/p2", "position": "An anomalous malīm has fatḥa on its first mīm and is understood as passive.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī derives it from līma. Al-Samīn calls it very anomalous: malūm is expected from a wāw-root, as maqūl and maṣūn are; he compares mashīb and muddaʿī with expected mashūb and madʿū. Abū Ḥayyān compares alīm; al-Ālūsī also explains it via līma."}]}

{"id": "37:142/q17", "question": "What preceding context do commentators bring to the swallowing?", "turns_on": "The cited notes explain different preceding words or the narrative gap.", "positions": [{"id": "37:142/q17/p1", "position": "The narrative omits intervening events for concision.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies a stalled ship, other ships passing, blame of a sinner, and lots."}, {"id": "37:142/q17/p2", "position": "The prior lot's idḥāḍ uses slipping as a metaphor for defeat or loss.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explains its literal and contextual senses."}, {"id": "37:142/q17/p3", "position": "A preceding lexical discussion contrasts injustice by inclination with constriction and burden.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ explains mayl and ʿawl in the preceding fragment."}]}
{"id": "37:143/q01", "question": "What does falawlā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported hallā generalization applies to this occurrence, especially to lawlā with prefixed fa; the notes question the generalization with other Qur'anic uses.", "positions": [{"id": "37:143/q01/p1", "position": "It introduces a counterfactual condition: without Jonah's glorification, the result in 37:144 would have followed.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says the following answer states what would have happened but for the condition. Suyūṭī cites other conditional lawlā constructions with omitted answers at 12:24, 28:82, and 28:10."}, {"id": "37:143/q01/p2", "position": "Al-Khalīl reportedly excepted Jonah's lawlā from a general Qur'anic sense of hallā, an exhortation; that generalization is disputed.", "reasons": "Ibn Barjān quotes al-Khalīl as saying all Qur'anic lawlā means hallā except Jonah's; al-Burhān questions the exception. {"id": "37:143/q02", "question": "How is the answer to lawlā construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "37:143/q02/p1", "position": "The lām in the following answer belongs to lawlā, not to anna.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī states that the lām does not govern anna; al-Naḥḥās agrees it marks lawlā's answer. {"id": "37:143/q03", "question": "Does kāna carry an independent meaning here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "37:143/q03/p1", "position": "On the reading of verbal praise, kāna may be superfluous: the condition is simply that Jonah was among those glorifying.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī presents this parsing specifically with the interpretation of spoken glorification."}]}
{"id": "37:143/q04", "question": "What does being among al-musabbiḥīn mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether tasbīḥ here is prayer, worship in general, remembrance and spoken praise, the particular plea of 21:87, or repentance; Ibn ʿAbbās's broad prayer gloss and the proper verbal sense are both cited.", "positions": [{"id": "37:143/q04/p1", "position": "Being among those who pray, including voluntary prayer.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Suddī, Ibn Masʿūd and others gloss tasbīḥ as prayer; an unnamed report specifies voluntary prayer. Al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī transmit Ibn ʿAbbās's broader assertion that every Qur'anic tasbīḥ means prayer. Al-Ālūsī warns that a technical sense needs no contextual clue only if it is the sole established sense; competing or figurative senses require a clue. The notes differ over whether this prayer occurred before or inside the fish, treated separately below."}, {"id": "37:143/q04/p2", "position": "Being a worshipper or one who fulfills God's due through established righteous deeds.", "reasons": "Wahb glosses the term as worshippers; Sahl says fulfillment of God's rights before affliction. This is a broader description than a particular utterance."}, {"id": "37:143/q04/p3", "position": "Remembrance and verbal glorification, declaring God free of what is unfitting to Him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī also reports a view explicitly preferring glorification to prayer. Al-Biqāʿī includes heart, tongue, and limbs."}, {"id": "37:143/q04/p4", "position": "Jonah's particular plea, 'There is no god but You; glory be to You; I was among the wrongdoers' (21:87).", "reasons": "Muqātil quotes the plea as a confession of God's oneness and purity and Jonah's wrongdoing. {"id": "37:143/q06", "question": "What in the wording suggests frequent or settled glorification?", "turns_on": "Whether frequency is conveyed by the intensive verbal form or by being counted among a definite class of habitual glorifiers.", "positions": [{"id": "37:143/q06/p1", "position": "Membership in the definite plural 'the glorifiers' presents a settled, abundant habit.", "reasons": "Al-Khafājī says naming Jonah as one of the group conveys deeper rootedness than simply calling him a glorifier; al-Ālūsī says the definite plural may signal constancy, and reads Qatāda as suggesting abundance. Al-Ālūsī rejects deriving repetition merely from the intensive verbal form, since one can say Subḥān Allāh once."}, {"id": "37:143/q06/p2", "position": "The intensive verbal form alone does not prove repeated glorification.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī objects that the act itself can be a single utterance of Subḥān Allāh; he instead allows the definite plural as evidence of habit."}]}
{"id": "37:143/q07", "question": "Why was Jonah released from distress?", "turns_on": "The notes differ over the timing of the effective worship and whether glorification by itself can account for rescue apart from divine grace and decree.", "positions": [{"id": "37:143/q07/p1", "position": "His established worship, prayer, and good deeds in ease supported him in hardship.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says God remembered earlier worship and rescued him. Qatāda's maxim says righteous deeds lift and support a person after a fall; al-Rabīʿ likewise cites past good.
